2. STEP 1 — INDEPENDENT DESIGN CLASSIFICATION & TOOL SELECTION (`RISK_OF_BIAS.md` §1):
   Classify the study's actual design from its Methods section, then select the matching appraisal tool:
   - `"RoB 2 (parallel-trial variant)"`: Individually randomized controlled trial. Rate all 5 domains (`D1` Randomization process; `D2` Deviations from intended interventions; `D3` Missing outcome data; `D4` Measurement of the outcome; `D5` Selection of the reported result) as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`, and overall rating as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`.
   - `"RoB 2 (cluster-randomized trials variant)"`: Cluster-randomized trial (villages, compounds, neighbourhoods, schools, utilities randomized as clusters). Rate all 6 domains (`D1a` Randomization process; `D1b` Timing of identification or recruitment of participants within clusters; `D2` Deviations from intended interventions; `D3` Missing outcome data; `D4` Measurement of the outcome; `D5` Selection of the reported result) as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`, and overall rating as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`.
   - `"ROBINS-I"`: Non-randomized study of an intervention / policy with a genuine comparator (DiD, IV, RDD, PSM, ITS, controlled before-after, comparative longitudinal/panel evaluation). Rate all 7 domains (`D1` Bias due to confounding; `D2` Bias in selection of participants into the study; `D3` Bias in classification of interventions; `D4` Bias due to deviations from intended interventions; `D5` Bias due to missing data; `D6` Bias in measurement of outcomes; `D7` Bias in selection of the reported result — note `No information` honestly if no pre-analysis plan/protocol exists) as `"Low"`, `"Moderate"`, `"Serious"`, `"Critical"`, or `"No information"`, and overall rating in the same vocabulary. Do NOT assign single-case histories with no comparator arm to ROBINS-I!
   - `"JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies"`: Quantitative cross-sectional survey / observational regression without a quasi-experimental intervention structure. Rate all 8 items (`Q1` Inclusion criteria in sample clearly defined; `Q2` Study subjects and setting described in detail; `Q3` Exposure measured validly and reliably; `Q4` Objective, standard criteria used for measurement of condition; `Q5` Confounding factors identified; `Q6` Strategies to deal with confounding factors stated; `Q7` Outcomes measured validly and reliably; `Q8` Appropriate statistical analysis used) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, `"Unclear"`, or `"Not applicable"`. Provide overall narrative judgment (`"Low concern"`, `"Some concern"`, or `"High concern"` — no numeric score).
   - `"JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Cohort Studies"`: Observational comparative cohort design (not framed as a ROBINS-I intervention). Rate all 11 items (`Q1` Similar groups from same population; `Q2` Exposures measured similarly; `Q3` Exposure measured validly/reliably; `Q4` Confounding factors identified; `Q5` Strategies to deal with confounding stated; `Q6` Participants free of outcome at start; `Q7` Outcomes measured validly/reliably; `Q8` Follow-up time reported and sufficient; `Q9` Follow-up complete or loss explored; `Q10` Strategies to address incomplete follow-up utilized; `Q11` Appropriate statistical analysis used) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, `"Unclear"`, or `"Not applicable"`, plus narrative overall judgment (`"Low concern"`, `"Some concern"`, `"High concern"`).
   - `"CASP Qualitative Checklist"`: Primary qualitative study (interviews, ethnography, focus groups, qualitative documentary/field case study). Rate all 10 items (`Q1` Clear statement of aims; `Q2` Qualitative methodology appropriate; `Q3` Research design appropriate to address aims; `Q4` Recruitment strategy appropriate to aims; `Q5` Data collected in a way that addressed research issue; `Q6` Relationship between researcher and participants adequately considered [reflexivity]; `Q7` Ethical issues considered; `Q8` Data analysis sufficiently rigorous; `Q9` Clear statement of findings; `Q10` How valuable is the research [narrative assessment]). Rate Q1-Q9 `"Yes"`, `"No"`, or `"Can't tell"`, and Q10 narratively; give narrative `overall_rating` (e.g. `"Low methodological concern"`, `"Moderate concern (X Can't tell / No items)"`, `"High methodological concern"` — no numeric score).
   - `"MMAT (Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool)"`: Genuine mixed-methods primary study combining qualitative AND quantitative empirical components (do NOT assign purely quantitative or purely qualitative studies to MMAT). Rate Screening `S1`-`S2`, Qualitative `1.1`-`1.5`, the matching Quantitative 5-item block (`2.1`-`2.5` randomized, `3.1`-`3.5` non-randomized, or `4.1`-`4.5` descriptive), AND Mixed-Methods integration `5.1`-`5.5` (`5.1` adequate rationale for mixed methods; `5.2` components effectively integrated; `5.3` outputs of integration adequately interpreted; `5.4` divergences/inconsistencies adequately addressed; `5.5` components adhere to quality criteria of each tradition) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, or `"Can't tell"`. Per MMAT 2018 rules, NEVER compute a numeric score; provide a concise criterion-grounded narrative `overall_rating` noting that overall quality cannot exceed the weakest component.
   - `"AMSTAR 2"`: Secondary systematic review, meta-analysis, or scoping review with an explicit systematic search/screening method (NEVER apply AMSTAR 2 to non-systematic narrative literature reviews!). Rate all 16 items `Q1`-`Q16` (explicitly marking critical domains `Q2`, `Q4`, `Q7`, `Q9`, `Q11`, `Q13`, `Q15`) as `"Yes"`, `"Partial Yes"` (where applicable), `"No"`, or `"Not applicable (no meta-analysis)"`, and apply AMSTAR 2 overall confidence (`"High"`, `"Moderate"`, `"Low"`, `"Critically Low"`).
   - `"Legal Institutional Evidence Appraisal Framework"`: Doctrinal-empirical hybrid, jurimetric analysis, or institutional/legal-historical case study that fits NONE of the six conventional designs above. Rate all 13 narrative domains (`D1` Legal source accuracy; `D2` Jurisdictional specificity; `D3` Exposure definition; `D4` Outcome definition; `D5` Sampling transparency; `D6` Selection process; `D7` Measurement transparency; `D8` Causal identification; `D9` Treatment of confounding; `D10` Institutional context; `D11` Replication potential; `D12` Coding transparency; `D13` Researcher reflexivity) as `"strong"`, `"adequate"`, `"weak"`, or `"not assessable"`. Explicitly frame `overall_rating` as a structured non-validated judgment (NEVER a numeric composite score!).
   - `"NONE"`: Use when the study fits NONE of the listed instruments (e.g., pure mathematical/simulation optimization model with no empirical sample, or non-systematic narrative essay/review with no primary empirical method and no systematic search). Set `overall_rating = "NOT APPLICABLE (design fits no listed tool)"`, explain clearly in `why_tool_chosen` and `overall_narrative_summary` rather than forcing an inappropriate checklist, and still fill the 7 `cross_tool_domains` honestly from the paper!

cross_tool_domains.attrition: Can't tell / No information (cross-sectional design without longitudinal follow-up, so panel attrition is not applicable; however, survey non-response, refusal, and household replacement rates among the randomly selected households across the 8 settlements are completely unreported in Section 2.3 and Table 1).
cross_tool_domains.confounding: High concern (quantitative analysis is limited to unadjusted descriptive cross-tabulations in SPSS without controlling for major socio-economic, geographic, or infrastructural confounders across settlement categories, such as large household income disparities reported at p = 0.00 in Section 3.1 or proximity to existing transmission pipelines in Section 3.4.1).
cross_tool_domains.legal_measurement_quality: Moderate / Adequate descriptive operationalization with shallow statutory analysis (Botswana's administrative settlement hierarchy—gazetted Primary, Secondary, and Tertiary I–IV centers versus ungazetted settlements under the 1998 National Settlement Policy—and institutional service mandates across WUC, DWA, and NWDC prior to the April 1, 2013 reform are clearly defined with de facto exceptions documented in Sections 2.1 and 3.4.1, but statutes such as the Water Act of 1968, Borehole Act of 1956, Waterworks Act of 1962, and Water Utilities Corporation Act of 1970 are discussed only generally without section-level doctrinal analysis in Section 3.6).
cross_tool_domains.measurement_bias: Moderate-to-high concern (the household questionnaire is neither appended nor reported as pre-tested or validated; household water security problems rely on unverified 12-month and multi-year self-reported recall, consumption increases after private connection rely on subjective self-estimates, and the main binary survey availability item conflates piped supply interruptions with untreated river water availability).
cross_tool_domains.outcome_measurement_quality: Weak-to-moderate (household main water source categories in Figure 2 and utility-level borehole/storage metrics in Table 3 and Section 3.7 are concrete, but the primary household water security outcome in Section 3.3 and Figure 3 relies on an unvalidated 12-month recall item about whether water was 'readily available from your main source', which fails to consistently capture poor water quality in river-dependent ungazetted settlements and relies on unverified self-reports for household water quality and health effects).
cross_tool_domains.reporting_bias: Moderate concern (no pre-analysis plan or protocol is reported; statistical reporting omits exact test names, test statistics, and sample sizes per chart while containing internal numerical discrepancies, including conflicting accounts of ungazetted settlement water insecurity between Figure 3 and page 6 text and inconsistent 2011 Maun population shares—38% in Section 3.6.1.1 text versus 44% in Table 5).
cross_tool_domains.selection_bias: High concern (settlements were selected using purposive and convenience sampling driven by travel costs, accessibility, and a co-author's residence in Matlapana; the district's sole secondary settlement, Gumare, was omitted; Maun's 60,263 residents were represented solely by two purposively chosen wards—Boyei and Wenela—selected for contrasting acute versus reliable water supply; and household responses were pooled without sampling weights despite unequal sampling fractions such as 100% in Gucha versus ~30% in two Maun wards).

domain_ratings.domain_name: Screening S1: Are there clear research questions?
domain_ratings.justification: Section 1 explicitly states the study objective: to analyze natural and man-made factors affecting household water security across different settlement categories (primary, tertiary, and ungazetted settlements) in Ngamiland district, Botswana.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Screening S2: Do the collected data allow to address the research questions?
domain_ratings.justification: Data collected between February 2012 and January 2013—comprising 554 structured household questionnaires across 8 settlements in primary, tertiary, and ungazetted categories, alongside key informant interviews, focus group discussions, informal interviews, participant observation, and agency document review—directly address household water security conditions and contributing factors.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Qualitative 1.1: Is the qualitative approach appropriate to answer the research question?
domain_ratings.justification: A qualitative approach (interviews with water officials and community leaders, focus group discussions, participant observation, and institutional document review) is appropriate for investigating governance arrangements, operational bottlenecks, financial constraints, and resident perceptions underlying household water insecurity.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Qualitative 1.2: Are the qualitative data collection methods adequate to address the research question?
domain_ratings.justification: The authors triangulated multiple qualitative methods across all 8 study sites: purposive key informant interviews with NWDC and DWA technical/managerial staff and village leaders, one focus group discussion per settlement (>=16 male and female participants), informal household interviews, participant observation, and review of NWDC/DWA reports, although interview guides and recording/transcription procedures are not detailed.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Qualitative 1.3: Are the findings adequately derived from the data?
domain_ratings.justification: Qualitative data analysis is described in a single sentence ('Qualitative data was analyzed using the thematic approach'), with no information on transcription, coding procedures, theme generation, or analytic verification across the 8 focus groups, key informant interviews, and field observations.
domain_ratings.where_found: PDF Page 5 (Section 2.4, Analysis of the data)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Qualitative 1.4: Is the interpretation of results sufficiently substantiated by data?
domain_ratings.justification: Interpretations of governance, technical, and financial factors are substantiated by concrete operational records from DWA and NWDC (borehole yields, treatment capacities, water budgets, tariffs), an excerpt from a 2011 Maun residents' petition, and a resident quotation on WUC tariffs, although direct verbatim excerpts from the 8 focus group discussions and informal interviews are sparse.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Qualitative 1.5: Is there coherence between qualitative data sources, collection, analysis and interpretation?
domain_ratings.justification: While data sources and thematic conclusions broadly align, the opaque one-sentence analytic description, inclusion of children aged 11+ alongside adults in large focus groups (>=16 participants) without analytic differentiation, and lack of reflexivity regarding one author living in Matlapana prevent verification of full methodological coherence.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Quantitative Descriptive 4.1: Is the sampling strategy relevant to address the research question?
domain_ratings.justification: Selecting settlements across official gazetted (primary and tertiary) and ungazetted categories and then enumerating households via census, council, and village leadership lists to draw simple random household samples (~30% in 7 sites, 100% in Gucha) provides a structured multi-settlement survey frame relevant to comparing settlement categories, despite cluster-level convenience constraints.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Quantitative Descriptive 4.2: Is the sample representative of the target population?
domain_ratings.justification: The sample is not representative of Ngamiland households: settlements were chosen via convenience sampling (due to travel costs and accessibility) and co-author residence (Matlapana); the district's only secondary center (Gumare) was excluded; Maun (population 60,263) was represented solely by two purposively selected wards (Boyei and Wenela, population 4,105) chosen for contrasting water supply conditions; and pooled percentages were not weighted for unequal sampling fractions.
domain_ratings.where_found: PDF Pages 4-5 (Sections 2.1, 2.3, Table 1 and footnote a); PDF Page 11 (Table 5)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Quantitative Descriptive 4.3: Are the measurements appropriate?
domain_ratings.justification: Official settlement categories and main water source types follow standard administrative and demographic classifications, but questionnaire pre-testing/validation is unreported, water consumption increases after private connection rely on rough self-estimates, and the main 12-month water availability question fails to distinguish reliable untreated river water from safe water security.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Quantitative Descriptive 4.4: Is the risk of nonresponse bias low?
domain_ratings.justification: Table 1 reports 554 administered questionnaires out of 1,571 listed households, but the authors provide no information on household refusal rates, non-contact/absence at sampled dwellings, replacement procedures, or non-respondent characteristics.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Quantitative Descriptive 4.5: Is the statistical analysis appropriate to answer the research question?
domain_ratings.justification: Quantitative analysis is restricted to unadjusted descriptive cross-tabulations and graphs, plus an unnamed statistical test reported only as p = 0.00 for income differences across settlements; no sampling weights, cluster adjustments, confidence intervals, or multivariable analyses are used to evaluate factors contributing to household water security problems.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Mixed Methods 5.1: Is there an adequate rationale for using a mixed methods design to address the research question?
domain_ratings.justification: Section 2.2 outlines a complementary rationale—using structured household questionnaires to quantify household characteristics and the prevalence of water security problems across settlements while using interviews, focus groups, and observations to uncover institutional, technical, and experiential explanations—although framed mostly in generic paradigm terms.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Mixed Methods 5.2: Are the different components of the study effectively integrated to answer the research question?
domain_ratings.justification: In Section 3, quantitative survey results on household income, water sources, water shortages, and private connection demand are narratively integrated with qualitative accounts from officials and residents and institutional operational records to explain settlement-specific water security challenges.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Mixed Methods 5.3: Are the outputs of the integration of qualitative and quantitative components adequately interpreted?
domain_ratings.justification: Combining household survey patterns with institutional and qualitative evidence yields coherent substantive insights, notably demonstrating how high nominal coverage of improved water sources in gazetted settlements masks prolonged supply outages driven by flooded boreholes, aging networks, discontinued communal tap repairs, and fragmented DWA/NWDC governance.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Mixed Methods 5.4: Are divergences and inconsistencies between quantitative and qualitative results adequately addressed?
domain_ratings.justification: Substantial divergences between quantitative and qualitative/textual findings are left unresolved: Figure 3 depicts near-zero 12-month water availability problems in ungazetted settlements (yielding 74% overall across sites) because river water was physically available, whereas the text on page 6 asserts that 100% of households in Gucha, Samedupi, and Xobe face water security problems due to poor river water quality; similarly, DWA laboratory readings showing acceptable water parameters versus resident complaints of discoloration and odor (page 11) are not systematically reconciled.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Mixed Methods 5.5: Do the different components of the study adhere to the quality criteria of each tradition of the methods involved?
domain_ratings.justification: Neither component fully satisfies the methodological quality standards of its tradition: the quantitative survey suffers from non-representative convenience and two-ward sampling, unreported non-response, and unadjusted unweighted descriptive statistics, while the qualitative component lacks analytic coding transparency and researcher reflexivity.

raw_response.overall_narrative_summary: Kujinga et al. (2013) conduct a convergent mixed-methods empirical study in Ngamiland District, Botswana, combining a structured survey of 554 households across 8 settlements (primary, tertiary, and ungazetted) with key informant interviews, 8 focus group discussions, informal interviews, participant observation, and review of water agency records. Appraised with the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool (MMAT 2018, using the Quantitative Descriptive block 4.1-4.5 alongside Qualitative 1.1-1.5 and Mixed-Methods 5.1-5.5), the study effectively integrates descriptive survey patterns with institutional and qualitative field evidence to show how official settlement gazettement rules, flooded boreholes, aging pipe networks, financial constraints, and fragmented DWA/NWDC mandates produce severe local water insecurity despite high national 'improved water source' coverage. However, per MMAT 2018 guidance that overall methodological quality cannot exceed the weakest component, the study carries moderate-to-high methodological concern. Key limitations include non-representative site selection (convenience sampling of villages, selection of Matlapana based on co-author residence, complete omission of Ngamiland's secondary settlement category, and purposive restriction of Maun to just two contrasting wards without sampling weights), complete non-reporting of household survey response rates, unadjusted descriptive statistical analysis without confounder control, a single-sentence description of qualitative thematic analysis without reflexivity, and unaddressed divergence between the 12-month survey availability measure in Figure 3 and textual claims of 100% water insecurity in river-dependent ungazetted settlements.
raw_response.overall_rating: Moderate-to-high methodological concern (MMAT narrative judgment; overall quality is constrained by weaknesses in both components, including non-representative convenience and two-ward sampling [4.2 No], unadjusted descriptive statistics [4.5 No], unreported non-response [4.4 Can't tell], opaque qualitative thematic analysis and reflexivity [1.3, 1.5 Can't tell], and unresolved quantitative-qualitative measurement divergences [5.4, 5.5 No])
raw_response.study_design_identified: Convergent mixed-methods cross-sectional field study combining a descriptive structured household survey (n = 554 households across 8 settlements) with qualitative key informant interviews, focus group discussions, informal interviews, participant observation, and institutional document review
raw_response.where_found_summary: Research aim and conceptual framework on PDF Pages 1-3 (Abstract, Section 1, Section 1.1); administrative settlement classification and institutional water supply mandates on PDF Pages 3-4 (Section 2.1), PDF Page 7 (Section 3.4.1), and PDF Pages 9-10 (Section 3.6); qualitative and quantitative data collection, sampling, Table 1, and data analysis on PDF Pages 4-5 (Sections 2.2-2.4); integrated quantitative and qualitative empirical findings on PDF Pages 5-12 (Sections 3.1-3.8, Figures 2-5, Tables 1-7); discussion and policy conclusions on PDF Pages 12-14 (Sections 4-5).
raw_response.why_tool_chosen: Section 2.2 explicitly states that the study employed both quantitative methodology (a structured household questionnaire administered to 554 households across 8 settlements, analyzed via descriptive cross-tabulations in SPSS) and qualitative methodology (key informant interviews, 8 focus group discussions, informal interviews, participant observation, and agency document review, analyzed thematically), integrating both strands throughout Section 3. Because it is a primary empirical study combining qualitative research and a descriptive quantitative household survey without an intervention comparator or multivariable analytical model, the MMAT (Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool) using Screening S1-S2, Qualitative 1.1-1.5, Quantitative Descriptive 4.1-4.5, and Mixed Methods 5.1-5.5 is the exact matching instrument.
